question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Portuguese Trade Network — Key Trading Ports]
options: Cochin (Kochi) — First major Portuguese factory on the Malabar Coast, established in 1500
Hormuz — Portuguese-controlled entrepôt for Persian Gulf trade (horses, silk, pearls)
Malacca — Hub of Southeast Asian spice trade, connecting the Spice Islands to the Indian Ocean network
Calicut — Portuguese established their main pepper trading factory here after signing a treaty with the Zamorin
wrong_fact: The Portuguese never established a successful trading factory in Calicut. The Zamorin of Calicut was consistently hostile; Vasco da Gama's first visit ended in conflict, and Cabral bombarded Calicut. Cochin, not Calicut, was the main pepper trading base on the Malabar Coast.
explanation: Cochin (Kochi) under the Raja of Cochin (a rival of the Zamorin) was the earliest Portuguese ally, hosting their first factory around 1500. Calicut was ruled by the Zamorin who, backed by Arab and Muslim merchants, opposed Portuguese intrusion. Portuguese-Calicut relations were marked by conflict, not treaties. Hormuz and Malacca were key nodes in the wider Indian Ocean trade network.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Portuguese Trade Network — Commodities and Regions]
options: Malabar Coast — Black pepper, cardamom, ginger (exported to Europe via Lisbon)
Spice Islands (Maluku/Moluccas) — Cloves, nutmeg, mace (accessed via Malacca)
Gujarat — Cotton textiles used as currency in East Africa and Southeast Asian intra-Asian trade
Coromandel Coast — Dominated by Portuguese spice plantations that directly competed with Malabar production
wrong_fact: There were no Portuguese spice plantations on the Coromandel Coast. Coromandel was known for cotton textiles, not spices. Portuguese presence there was through trading factories. Spice production remained in Malabar (pepper) and the Maluku Islands (cloves, nutmeg). Portuguese did not cultivate spice plantations on Coromandel.
explanation: Portuguese intra-Asian trade worked by using Gujarat textiles to buy Malabar pepper, Maluku spices, Chinese silk, and Japanese silver. The Coromandel Coast (present Tamil Nadu–Andhra) was a textile zone; Portuguese had factories at Sao Thome de Meliapor (Madras) and Masulipatnam for cotton cloth trade, not spice cultivation.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Portuguese Trade Network — Ports and their Regional Trade Connections]
options: Hormuz — Connected the Persian Gulf horse trade; Arabian horses were imported to Deccan Sultanates via this route
Mozambique and Kilwa — East African ports in the Portuguese network supplying gold and ivory from the African interior
Nagasaki — Portuguese traded silver for Chinese silk there; Japan was incorporated into the Portuguese trade network in the 16th century
Macao — Portuguese established a permanent settlement here in 1557 as a base for China trade; they exported Chinese porcelain and silk to Europe
wrong_fact: Nagasaki was not the initial Portuguese port in Japan. Portuguese first reached Japan in 1543 and traded at Tanegashima and later at Hirado. Nagasaki was not developed as a port until the 1570s, and it was not a Portuguese-controlled port — it was a Japanese port open to Portuguese traders. The Portuguese were expelled from Japan in 1639.
explanation: Portuguese reached Japan in 1543 (Tanegashima). They traded at Hirado and later Nagasaki (opened 1571). The silver-for-silk trade between Japan and China via Portuguese middlemen was highly profitable. However, saying 'Nagasaki' as a Portuguese trade centre with the implication of it being like Macao (a permanent settlement) is historically imprecise — Portugal had no formal territorial possession in Japan. Macao (1557) was indeed a genuine Portuguese settlement for China trade.
